newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan stops short of condemning Malaysia arrests.
newsitem.headline: Japan stops short of condemning Malaysia arrests.

text.p: Japan on Monday stopped short of condemning Malaysia's brief detention of five Japanese participants who attended a controversial conference in Kuala Lumpur on human rights in East Timor.
Government officials called the detention a domestic issue and said Japan needed to check whether any infringement of rights took place before considering if a protest was in order.

"It's a domestic issue," top government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama told a news conference. "They...temporarily detained a number of people." Kajiyama was commenting on calls by the Japanese branch of Amnesty International for a strong protest from Tokyo over the incident.

The local head of the human rights organisation, Edith Hanson, urged Tokyo to protest against what she said was interference with the conference and the detention of 47 foreign participants by Malaysian authorities on Saturday.
"The (Malaysian) government has evidently violated human rights. Its actions are against the rules of the international community," she told reporters.
"We are not sure whether the Malaysian government actually abused its legal rights to detain and deport (the activists)," a Japanese Foreign Ministry official said.
"We must check on this before considering any measures of protest," he added.
The conference was held ahead of the anniversary on Tuesday of the 1991 killing by Indonesian troops of at least 50 demonstrators in East Timor's capital of Dili.
Roman Catholic Bishop Nobuo Soma, the 80-year-old leader of the Japanese delegation to the conference, said he was shocked and dismayed by the interference.
"I don't have the faintest idea why the conference had to be crushed," an angry Soma told Reuters.
"The organisers obtained permission from the Malaysian government," he said after arriving at Osaka's Kansai International Airport on Monday.
Three other members of the delegation have also returned to Japan and the fifth was on his way back via Manila.

The delegates, from 18 non-governmental organisations, were held by Malaysian immigration authorities after the meeting was stormed by a youth group loyal to Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad.
Twenty-six local activists and 36 foreigners were released on Sunday.
"We were shoved into cage-like prison vans and kept exposed to the public eye for many hours," Roman Catholic nun Yoko Nakamura said.
Indonesia invaded East Timor in 1975 after the abrupt departure of its Portuguese colonisers and now rules the territory in defiance of the United Nations.
